title: Living ashtpadi 8
hookLine: the brahm giaanee is a portrait to grow into, not a title to claim

lines: A CHILD IN HER FATHER'S SHOES.
cards: A child puts on her father's shoes and clomps around the kitchen. They're enormous. She trips.
Everyone laughs, and nobody thinks she's pretending to be him. She's trying them on, leaning toward a size she'll grow into one day.
There's a world of difference between that child and someone who buys a uniform and starts giving orders. One is growing. The other is claiming.
Ashtpadi eight's portrait of the brahm giaanee can be worn either way. Only one of those ways fits the portrait.

teach.b: Ashtpadi eight paints its portrait for eight stanzas. True in mind and mouth. A lotus in water.

The sun, the wind, the earth, the fire. And more: the God-conscious one is filled with humility, gareebee, the word that also means being poor, low, unassuming. The God-conscious one delights in doing good for others.
Friend and enemy look the same to them.

Then, deep in the ashtpadi, a line that stops the whole thing becoming a checklist: only a brahm giaanee knows the state of a brahm giaanee. You can't assess it from outside, and you certainly can't award it to yourself.

teach.h: TO CLAIM IT IS TO LACK IT.
teach.b: Put the humility and that line together, and a quiet logic appears: anyone who announces I am a brahm giaanee has just shown a lack of the humility at its heart.
So ashtpadi eight reads best as a mirror and a direction, never as a label.

teach.h: ONE QUALITY, A LITTLE AT A TIME.
teach.b: Living it means picking one quality, the earth's patience, the lotus's dryness, the wind's fairness, and growing into it, a little, the way a child grows into shoes. And this is where the week ends.
Seven days ago, the holy company: the face growing bright, ego leaving quietly, company chosen like food. Then the brahm giaanee: true inside and out, a lotus, and the earth. A week of good people.

how: Sikhs read ashtpadi eight of Sukhmani Sahib as a portrait of qualities to cultivate, and teachers caution against anyone claiming the title brahm giaanee for themselves.

o: shame at being seen as poor
a vow to give away all you own

p: the same to digger and anointer

s: ashtpadi eight is a checklist for awarding the title brahm giaanee
it says only a brahm giaanee knows that state; it can't be assessed or claimed.
the portrait includes humility and delight in doing good for others
gareebee, and eagerness to do good.
announcing 'I am a brahm giaanee' shows a lack of the portrait's humility
humility is at the portrait's heart.

games.q: you've read ashtpadi eight and recognize yourself in one line. what now?
o: tell your friends you're nearly a brahm giaanee.
pick one quality and quietly grow into it.
decide it's too high and give up.
games.why: the portrait is a direction, not a label: grow into it, a little at a time.

practice: Choose one quality from the portrait: the lotus, untouched in the mess; the earth, the same to the one who digs and the one who honors; the wind, fair to king and beggar; or gareebee, humble and unassuming.
Don't pick the hardest; pick the one that feels like a shoe slightly too big, and breathe in its name. If you pray, you can ask for help to grow.

wordCard.voice: Gareebee, humility, lowliness. The brahm giaanee is a portrait to grow into, with gareebee at its heart, never a title to claim.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: gareebee, humility, lowliness; in ashtpadi eight, the brahm giaanee is filled with it.

carryVoice: Your line: grow into it. A portrait to lean toward, never a title to claim. A week, done, and a good one.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
